picks.style: greek oracular chant, lyre and low drone, veiled female voice, slow, incantatory
picks.why: The Sibyl names her own half-mortal birth, then speaks from her tombstone: 'A maiden once gifted with voice, but now for ever voiceless.'

picks.style: delphic prophecy chant, aulos and hand drum, harsh male voice, ominous, building
picks.why: Demeter's threat to the acorn-eaters of Phigaleia — famine, cannibalism, and a bargain, all in hexameters.

picks.style: votive hymn, kithara and soft percussion, clear tenor, measured, elegiac
picks.why: A dead man's shield speaks from the wall, and Homer is told he has no fatherland, only a motherland.

picks.style: old english scop, bowed lyre and frame drum, low male chant, stark, declamatory
picks.why: 'Hark! We have heard it' — the alliterative opening sets the persecution and the whole world of the poem in sixteen lines.

picks.style: dark ritual chant, bowed lyre and rasping drone, growling male voice, ominous, driving
picks.why: The devil's inventory of his own work: strife poured from a cup in the wine-hall, souls sent out by the sword.

picks.style: anglo-saxon elegy, solo bowed lyre, hollow male voice, slow, cold
picks.why: Drowned on the swan's road, with no treasure-giver to hand them apple-gold from the beer-bench — the great Old English image of the lost hall.

picks.style: gothic chamber song, viola da gamba and chamber organ, dark tenor, slow, brooding
picks.why: The invocation of Melancholy from her yew-bowered cave, with Ruin sitting among sunk magnificence.

picks.style: winter nocturne, solo cello and muted piano, low male voice, unhurried, wistful
picks.why: 'I choose the pale December's foggy glooms' — dying embers and the cricket's drowsy dirge, a complete mood in itself.

picks.style: gothic ode, tremolo strings and distant horn, urgent tenor, restless, eerie
picks.why: The traveller shut alive in a catacomb while the mummies seem to rise — the strongest image in the poems.

picks.style: pastoral folk ballad, acoustic guitar and fiddle, warm female vocal, unhurried, sweet
picks.why: Built on 'Sweet is...' anaphora — village dance, labourer's fire, concrete and already half a song.

picks.style: hymn-metre reflection, parlour piano and soft strings, gentle soprano, steady, hopeful
picks.why: Clean common-metre stanzas on light breaking through cloud, ending 'Hope's bright torch more clearly shines, amidst surrounding gloom.'

picks.style: gothic ballad, harp and low strings, hushed female voice, mysterious, slow
picks.why: The white-robed bard appearing out of black night with a flaming brand — the one genuinely visual passage.

picks.style: georgian nocturne ode, chamber strings and flute, calm tenor, slow, tender
picks.why: Night falling over the plain, the woodman's axe silent, and the slave briefly forgetting his chains.

picks.style: valentine air with refrain, harpsichord and recorder, light soprano, dancing, playful
picks.why: Real refrain lines that circle back: 'Only while we love we live, love alone can pleasure give.'

picks.style: baroque love song, lute and viol, ardent tenor, flowing, warm
picks.why: Leander crossing the roaring sea for the torch hung out of the tower — a whole myth in six lines.

picks.style: roman martial recitation, war horn and low drum, commanding baritone, stately, resolute
picks.why: Pyrrhus refusing ransom — 'the sword, not gold, weigh the outcome' — and then the lamp lit from another's lamp.

picks.style: revolutionary art song, solo piano and cello, declamatory baritone, slow, gathering
picks.why: Only candidate; the Coleridge lines on France stamping her strong foot carry it.

picks.style: greek lyric fragment, solo lyre, single unaccompanied male voice, sparse, aphoristic
picks.why: Only candidate; the Simonides fragment on the foursquare man and Pittacus' 'Hard to be good' — the axis of the dialogue.
